ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Neurology (headache medicine) Consultation — Friedrich Nietzsche

code.originalText: Two-week review of the headache diary, the MRI and the comprehensive eye examination, seen the same day by headache medicine: diagnosis, withdrawal of the overused tablets and preventive treatment

text.paragraph: Headache on about 20 days a month with nausea, vomiting and light sensitivity, mostly right-sided, since childhood and more frequent over the past year, with a butalbital combination taken on most headache days, in a 36-year-old writer with high myopia. Please confirm the diagnosis and advise on withdrawal of the tablets and on preventive treatment. [S]
Urgency: Within two weeks, on the day of his two-week primary care review, with the headache diary, the MRI and the eye examination. [S]

list.item: Do his headaches meet ICHD-3 criteria for chronic migraine, and is medication overuse headache present?
Do the MRI, the syphilis serology and the eye findings explain or exclude a secondary cause, given the right-sided pattern, the unequal pupils and his father's illness?
How should the butalbital combination be withdrawn safely, and what acute treatment should replace it?
Which preventive treatment fits a writer with high myopia and constipation?
How should we follow him while he moves between a mountain village in summer and the coast in winter?

text.paragraph: Mr. Nietzsche, a 36-year-old writer and former professor, is seen at the request of Dr. Ellison-Mbatha with a 14-day diary, an MRI done this morning and a comprehensive eye examination done today. Headaches began in childhood and have grown more frequent and severe in adult life; for at least eight months he has had headache on about 20 days a month. In the diary, headache came on 10 of 14 days: on 7 it was moderate or severe, throbbing, mostly over the right forehead and eye, worse with walking uphill and reading, with light and noise sensitivity and nausea, and vomiting on 3, lasting six hours to two days; on 3 it was a milder pressure. He has never had an aura. He took the butalbital combination on 9 days and ibuprofen on 2. He has no history of seizures, drinks little and takes no other sedatives. He sleeps four to five hours and has occasional constipation. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Friedrich Nietzsche was born on October 15, 1844, in Röcken, near Leipzig, where his father was a Lutheran minister. [D]

His father, a Lutheran pastor, died in 1849, when his son was four, after about a year of seizures and progressive neurological deficits; an autopsy described "softening" of the brain. Nietzsche later wrote that his father died "in his six-and-thirtieth year"; medical accounts give his age as 36. The cause was not established. [D]

He had severe myopia, worse in the right eye, and a right pupil larger than the left, both noted in early childhood; at about five an eye examination found that the right eye needed a very strong (six-dioptre) lens. By about 30 the right eye was functionally blind, and in 1878 an ophthalmologist found fluid in the right retina and diagnosed retinitis (central chorioretinitis). [D]

Severe headaches began in his school years; at nine he was already missing school because of them. They were mainly right-sided, frontal and above the eye, came with sensitivity to light and with nausea and vomiting, and grew more severe in adult life. [D]

In 1869, at 24, he was appointed to the chair of classical philology at Basel. Ill health led to sick leave in 1871 and again in 1876 to 1877, and in 1879 he resigned his professorship and received a small pension; he never held another post. [D]

Looking back in 1888, he wrote that in 1879, in his "six-and-thirtieth year," he reached "the lowest point in my vitality," when "my eyes could distinguish nothing that lay three paces away from me"; he resigned at Basel, and the next winter, his "first winter in Genoa," he wrote Dawn "in the midst of the agony of a headache which lasted three days, accompanied by violent nausea." [D]

After resigning he settled into a pattern of spending winters near the Mediterranean, usually in Italy, and summers in Sils Maria. After an unsuccessful spring taking the waters at Recoaro, he went to the Upper Engadine at the beginning of July 1881 and rented a modest room in Sils Maria, hoping the dry, sunny climate would relieve his headaches; he kept a strict daily schedule with five to seven hours of walking, filling notebooks as he went. [D]
By his own admission he had gonorrhea twice in his twenties; whether either infection was in fact syphilis could not have been told apart reliably at the time. [D]

code.displayName: Relevant Diagnostic Tests and/or Laboratory Data

list.item: Chronic migraine without aura (G43.709). ICHD-3 criteria for chronic migraine are met: headache on 15 or more days a month for more than three months, with features of migraine without aura (throbbing, moderate to severe, worse with activity, with nausea, vomiting and light and noise sensitivity) on at least 8 days a month. The milder pressure days are part of the same disorder. Cluster headache and hemicrania continua do not fit: there are no tearing, redness or other autonomic signs, and the pain is not continuous. [S]

Medication overuse headache (G44.40). Present: a combination analgesic on 10 or more days a month for more than three months in a person with 15 or more headache days a month. Butalbital is a barbiturate and should be tapered rather than stopped at once; ibuprofen can be stopped now. [S]

Secondary causes (G43.709). The strongly right-sided pattern and the rising frequency justified imaging, and the MRI with contrast shows no structural lesion, including none behind the right eye. Nonreactive treponemal and nontreponemal tests exclude syphilis as a cause of the headaches or the pupils, and no lumbar puncture is needed. The unequal pupils, both briskly reactive and present since early childhood, are long-standing and benign, and the poor right eye is explained by myopic macular atrophy. His father's illness cannot be diagnosed from the record; nothing in his own history, examination or MRI suggests an inherited neurological disease, and no genetic testing is indicated. [S]

Preventive treatment (G43.709). Prevention is indicated for chronic migraine with severe disability. A CGRP monoclonal antibody is a first-line option under the 2024 American Headache Society position statement and the European Headache Federation guideline, which also supports starting it with withdrawal in medication overuse headache. Galcanezumab suits him: monthly self-injection travels well between his summer and winter homes, and it causes constipation less often than erenumab. Topiramate is a poor fit because it can slow word-finding and concentration and, rarely, cause acute myopia with angle-closure glaucoma. OnabotulinumtoxinA is effective in chronic migraine but needs injections every 12 weeks at a center; it is the next option if the antibody is not enough. [S]

Pathologic myopia and headache (H44.2E1). Eye strain from uncorrected anisometropia can add to headache on reading days; contact lenses should make reading more comfortable. Flashes and floaters in a highly myopic eye need same-day examination and should not be mistaken for aura. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Ellison-Mbatha's intake note and the diary. MRI of the brain and orbits without and with contrast: normal brain, pituitary and optic nerves, no mass or white matter lesions; elongated globes with a right posterior staphyloma. Treponemal antibody 0.12 (nonreactive) and RPR nonreactive. Eye examination today: best corrected vision 20/100 right and 20/20 left, refraction about -13.50 and -6.25, intraocular pressure 15 and 14 mmHg, pathologic myopia of the right eye with macular atrophy and no neovascularization, no retinal breaks. MIDAS 74 and HIT-6 68 at intake; PHQ-9 7, GAD-7 6. Blood pressure 116/74 and pulse 66 today. [S]

list.item: Stop ibuprofen now. Replace as-needed butalbital combination tablets with a scheduled taper: one tablet twice a day for 7 days, once a day for 7 days, every other day for 7 days, then stop. Expect worse headache for one to two weeks; seek same-day care for tremor, sweating, agitation, confusion or a seizure. A nurse phone check at the end of the first week. [S]

Galcanezumab 240 mg subcutaneously today as a loading dose, then 120 mg every four weeks; judge the effect at about three months, seeking at least half as many migraine days and fewer than 15 headache days a month. [S]

Acute treatment during and after the taper: naproxen 500 mg with metoclopramide 10 mg early in an attack, no more than two days a week; add sumatriptan 100 mg once the taper is complete, no more than eight triptan days a month; no butalbital, opioids or caffeine combination products. [S]
OnabotulinumtoxinA if the antibody fails or the response fades. [S]
Count every acute-medicine day in the diary; review at four weeks and at eight weeks with the MIDAS, HIT-6, PHQ-9 and GAD-7. [S]
Contact lenses for both eyes, an Amsler grid for the right eye, and same-day eye care for new flashes, floaters or a shadow. [S]
CBT-I for insomnia, with no sedative sleeping tablets; regular meals, a fixed rising time, and his daily walks. [S]
Before he leaves for the winter, a three-month review and a written plan, with his diary and injection supplies, for care near his winter home. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Ellison-Mbatha, who saw him the same day. The diagnosis, the MRI and serology results, and the reasons for each step were explained to Mr. Nietzsche, who asked whether his headaches meant an illness like his father's and was reassured by the normal results. He chose galcanezumab after weighing it against topiramate and onabotulinumtoxinA, and the first dose was given in clinic. [S]

Follow-up: Dr. Ellison-Mbatha continues care at four and eight weeks and at three months; headache medicine will see him again if prevention fails, the pattern changes, or onabotulinumtoxinA is needed. [S]
